vignette:
Mr. Tran is a sixty-six-year-old roofer who has worked on roofs across the San Fernando Valley since he immigrated from Vietnam in the early 1980s. He still drives his own truck, though his son has taken over most of the heavy shingle work. That morning, about three and a half years ago, started like any other-cloudless sky, slight breeze, the familiar sting of tar and solvent in the air. He was re-sealing a flat commercial roof, applying a rubberized coating with a heavy roller. The label on the drum warned about ventilation, but he had done this a thousand times. He remembers the way the wind shifted, pushing the milky white fumes directly into his face, and the moment his lungs seized. He doubled over, coughing, gasping, his throat feeling like it had been rubbed with glass. His crew helped him down and called the foreman. He sat in the back of the truck for an hour, sipping water, telling himself it would pass.

It didn't pass. The burning sensation in his throat faded over the next week, but something else settled into his chest-a tightness that never entirely loosened. At first, he thought it was his heart or his age. He went to a doctor, who said his lungs were clear. But the feeling remained. Now, whenever the wind picks up or he catches the smell of fresh paint or gasoline from a lawnmower, his breathing quickens. More than the physical sensation, it is the wave of panic that arrives without warning: the flash of that white cloud, the helplessness of being unable to pull in air, the certainty that something inside him has been permanently damaged.

He still does roofs, but he has changed the way he works. He refuses to use any product that comes in a white drum, even if it is the same chemical under a different label. His crew laughs at him for being superstitious, but the sight of that shape on a delivery truck makes his stomach knot. He checks the weather obsessively before every job, insisting on days when the wind is steady from the south, which he maps in his head as "clean air on the west side of the building." His son tries to be patient, but Mr. Tran can see the frustration in his eyes when he stops the whole crew to reposition a bucket because the breeze is coming from a different direction.

At home, his wife notices he no longer sits outside on the patio in the evenings. She used to enjoy watching him tinker with her potted plants, but now he stays indoors, the sliding door shut, the ceiling fan off because the current stirs up dust. He has become silent during dinner, his mind replaying the few seconds before the wind shifted. He wonders if he had turned his face away sooner, if he had worn a different mask, if the foreman had warned him about the drum's label. These thoughts circle and circle, and he has learned to keep them inside because when he tries to explain the burning or the panic, his wife's face softens into pity, and then she sighs. The pity makes him feel more alone than the symptoms do.

Last week, a neighbor's truck idled in the driveway while Mr. Tran was washing his car. The exhaust smelled like the rolled-on solvent, and he found himself on his hands and knees in the garage, coughing before any real fumes had reached him. He stayed there, hands pressed to the concrete floor, until the truck pulled away. That night he told his wife he was just tired from work. He did not tell her about the coughing or the way his ears rang for an hour afterward. He does not know if this is something that will ever loosen its hold. For now, he goes to work, he avoids the white drums, and he waits for winter, when the wind rarely blows at all.
